en: This circuit, however, requires a constant renewal of meaning<1><2>275</2></1>. Cultural meaning flows incessantly from the culturally constituted world to goods and from goods <3>p. 256</3> to the consumer, through instruments of transfer and consumption rituals <4>McCracken</4><5>(McCracken, 1986, p. 71)</5>. Advertising works as a conduit through which meaning is continually poured into goods, informing the public of the current stock of available meanings and operating as a lexicon<6><7>276</7></6> of prevailing cultural senses <8>McCracken</8><9>(McCracken, 1986, p. 75-76)</9>. Moreover, culture operates as lens and as <10>blueprint</10><11><12>277</12></11> of action, determining the coordinates of social action and specifying the behaviors and objects that enter it as legitimate references <13>McCracken</13><14>(McCracken, 1986, p. 72)</14>.

Renewal is not optional because part of meaning is perishable<1><2>278</2></1>. If certain symbolic attributes “spoil” over time, the consumer is led to draw meaning from <3>p. 257</3> his possessions repeatedly, resorting to rituals that extract these special and perishable properties from possessions, making them come alive, even if for a brief interval, in the individual's experience <4>McCracken</4><5>(McCracken, 1986, p. 79)</5>. On platforms, this describes the pressure not to fall behind as a ritualized renewal of perishable signs. Updating one's repertoire becomes a discipline of presence, and the discipline of presence sustains the toll by converting the renewal of signals into a practical obligation of attendance under administered visibility.

From this perspective, control of access is not exhausted in price or contract when demand itself is organized before it presents itself as preference. In ecosystems governed by curation, <1>ranking</1> and windows of appearance, the relevant competition migrates to the dispute over control of discovery. Whoever controls the paths of visibility controls the practical formation of desire, since they decide what enters the horizon of comparison and what remains invisible. Power ceases to be merely selling, and becomes defining what appears as worthy of investment, which trajectories are rewarded, which signals become necessary for belonging and which paths of enjoyment impose themselves as the default route.

Here, Appadurai's contribution closes the mechanism by treating demand as the economic expression of the political logic of consumption and by insisting that consumption is social, relational and active. Demand<1><2>279</2></1> is a socially regulated and generated impulse, and not an artifact of individual whims <3>Appadurai</3><4>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 31-32)</4>.

This point puts choice back in its place. The abstraction of the isolated rational individual is unworkable when millions share consumption and reciprocally transform the field of meanings. The intelligibility of the social world depends on visible markings and on public <1>p. 258</1> categories fixed by conventions, and consumption is precisely the mechanism that makes judgments firm and visible by classifying people and events, requiring “complaisant” peers for public categories to be maintained or changed <2>Isherwood</2><3>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. viii-ix; p. 43; p. 45)</3>. On platforms, curation, metrics and windows take on this function of public fixation, converting visibility into performed consensus and consensus into support for the toll.

If the platform governs regimes of value and scripts of choice through rules of visibility and continuous updating of the desirable repertoire, it also governs the way in which the immaterial object is promised, perceived and enjoyed. The promise of the good includes expectations of social utility that depend on public visibility and collective validation in the ecosystem. Unilateral changes that reconfigure criteria of display, circulation, rarity and grammars of comparison are not neutral “cosmetics”, since they bear upon the semiotic core that makes up the social utility of the IOC and structures the consumer's decision. In this framework, governance of signification ceases to be a backdrop and becomes part of the governance of the good itself, since it alters the conditions under which the item exists as a relevant difference, as socially perceived rarity and as a public marker of position.

In this framing, what is usually perceived as individual preference comes to be described as a discipline of perception and permanence, operated by curation and regimes of appearance that define the horizon of the desirable and the grammar of belonging. In markets of immaterials, economic stability depends not only on price and clause, but on continued control of the field in which permanence is decided in practice, through attention and visibility.

The conversion of technical abundance into socially perceived scarcity is anchored in three coupled mechanisms. First, by validation through consensus, in which metrics, display and circulation produce performed recognition and make value “seem” natural. Second, by discipline of presence, in which the perishability of meaning and the timing of enjoyment turn the updating of repertoire into a practical obligation of attendance. And third, by an exit cost enlarged by reputational and belonging losses, such that the act of leaving the ecosystem implies not only losing utility, but losing social legibility and recognizable position. The result is an identity captivity, in which the toll stabilizes as a fee for maintaining one's place, not as the one-off price of an item.

The shift to the semiotic key is thus ripe. The mechanism described explains how visibility, updating and belonging stabilize recurring revenue and enlarge the exit cost. What remains is to advance, with greater granularity, to the concrete operations of interface, curation and circulation through which the platform produces meaning and discipline of <1>p. 259</1> presence, and to the legal qualification of these arrangements when they cease to be ordinary management of the service and come to constitute abusive teleology, by reordering promise, enjoyment and the minimum preservation of legitimately expected value over time.<2> </2>

This analytical perspective finds a structural, non-psychologizing formulation in <1>The World of Goods: Towards an </1> <2>Anthropology of Consumption</2>, by Mary Douglas and Baron Isherwood (1996), originally published in 1979. Instead of treating consumption as a moral caricature or as a sum of individual impulses, the work reinserts goods into the social process and describes consumption as language and as everyday ritual. The methodological inversion proposed by Douglas and Isherwood appears as an explicit command. The target is the impoverished reading of consumption as irrationality, excess or mere satisfaction of material needs. The central move consists in suspending, for long enough, the vocabulary of biological utility, in order to observe what goods do as operators of thought, classification and communication. The reference to Lévi-Strauss works as a theoretical framing, since, just as certain animals are “good to think” in the logic of totemism, commodities can also be “good to think” when treated as a medium of symbolic work. “Forget the idea of consumer irrationality. Forget that commodities are good for eating, clothing, and shelter; forget their usefulness and try instead the idea that commodities are good for thinking; treat them as a nonverbal medium for the human creative faculty” <3>Isherwood</3><4>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 40-41)</4>. The conceptual consequence is significant, since goods cease to be read as things that merely “serve” and come to be understood as a nonverbal medium of cultural elaboration. This opens room for understanding consumption as everyday cognitive infrastructure, in which choosing, using and displaying goods is not moral noise in rationality, but one of the ways in which social categories become practicable. The “creative faculty”, in this register, is not reduced to artistic creativity, but designates the ordinary capacity to make the world intelligible through materialized signs. <5>↩</5>

Douglas and Isherwood go further by formulating the perspective of goods as an information system. The point is not merely that “objects communicate”, but that this communication is structural and relational, and depends on the whole. The isolated item is semantically incomplete, since meaning emerges from the reciprocal position among goods, as happens in a grammar or in a musical harmony. At this point, the authors consolidate the argument with two images that organize the reasoning, namely, the idea of a system that “monitors its own performance” and the analogy with music, in which the minimal unit is not the note, but the relation between notes. “The goods are both the hardware and the software, so to speak, of an information system whose principal concern is to monitor its own performance. […] The counterargument proposed here is that all goods carry meaning, but none by itself. […] The meaning is in the relations between all the goods, just as music is in the relations marked out by the sounds and not in any one note” <1>Isherwood</1><2>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 49)</2>. This redefines what “value” is on the anthropological plane. Value comes to function as an effect of insertion in a series, and not as a physical attribute of the object. A good is “worth” something because it occupies an intelligible place in an arrangement of differences, complementarities and hierarchies. Consequently, any alteration in the arrangement, whether in what appears together, in what is comparable, in what is rare, in what is seen as a “peer”, modifies what the good “says”. The unit of analysis ceases to be the item and becomes the grammar of the collection. <3>↩</3>

In <1>The Social Life of Things</1> (1986), Arjun Appadurai proposes understanding the commodity as a situated and transitory condition, defined by the social arenas of exchange, and not as a fixed category restricted to capitalism. Titled <2>Introduction: Commodities and the Politics of Value</2>, the essay opens the volume edited by Appadurai, which gathers essays in anthropology and history aimed at shifting the gaze from exchange as abstraction to the things themselves in circulation, treating commodities as objects endowed with a “social life” and with trajectories that vary according to cultural and historical contexts. Instead of presupposing value as an inherent attribute of the object or as a simple mechanical effect of the market, the volume emphasizes that value is produced and stabilized in social regimes of recognition, circulation and classification. <3>↩</3>

Appadurai begins with an operation of conceptual cleansing. Before dealing with circulation, commodity and regimes, he redefines what is understood by value, precisely to prevent the analysis from falling back into an ontology of the object. The starting point is Simmel. Value is not an inherent property of the thing, but a situated judgment, formulated by subjects and made effective by conditions of demand and exchange. The economic object, therefore, does not possess absolute value as a mechanical effect of desire. It is demand, as the basis of a real or imagined exchange, that invests the thing with value. Next comes the decisive inversion. It is not utility or scarcity that explain exchange, but exchange that defines the practical parameters of utility and scarcity. “Value, for Simmel, is never an inherent property of objects, but is a judgment made about them by subjects. […] Thus, the economic object does not have an absolute value as a result of the demand for it, but the demand, as the basis of a real or imagined exchange, endows the object with value. It is exchange that sets the parameters of utility and scarcity, rather than the other way round, and exchange that is the source of value…” <1>Appadurai</1><2>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 3-4)</2>. With this shift, “commodity” ceases to be a moral or natural category and comes to designate a relational and historical condition. Value becomes intelligible as an effect of practices, expectations and arenas of exchange. The analysis of the economic, consequently, shifts to the frameworks that make exchange possible, that is, to mechanisms that stabilize judgments of value, instead of explaining value “from inside” the object. <3>↩</3>

Having set aside the idea of value as essence, Appadurai formulates a concept to face a recurring problem in economic anthropology. Exchanges occur even when there is no dense and shared cultural consensus about “what is worth how much”. Cross-cultural trade, exchanges under necessity and circulation between heterogeneous and asymmetrical groups require an analytical language that depends neither on cultural homogeneity nor on fully shared assumptions. In this context, Appadurai prefers to speak of regimes of value, not to presuppose a unified cultural system, but to describe variable degrees of evaluative coherence, sufficient to enable equivalences and hierarchies in diverse situations. The formulation is explicit: “I prefer to use the term regimes of value, which does not imply that every act of commodity exchange presupposes a complete cultural sharing of assumptions, but rather that the degree of value coherence may be highly variable from situation to situation, and from commodity to commodity. A regime of value, in this sense, is consistent with both very high and very low sharing of standards by the parties to a particular commodity exchange” <1>Appadurai</1><2>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 14-15)</2>. The concept offers a tool for seeing value as an operational grammar, composed of standards and criteria that need not be fully consensual in order to work, provided they produce enough practical coherence to guide equivalences, distinctions and disputes. Regime of value, thus, does not describe cultural harmony, but the capacity of an arena of exchange to make value “operate” under friction, asymmetry and disagreement. <3>↩</3>

In the conclusion, Appadurai names the structural link between value and exchange, which in everyday life tends to remain invisible, since custom takes on an appearance of neutrality. This link is politics, understood in a broad sense, as relations, assumptions and contests tied to power. Routine exchange only seems “natural” because it depends on agreements about the desirable, about what counts as a reasonable sacrifice in a transaction and, above all, about who is authorized to exercise effective demand in given circumstances. For this reason, value and exchange are not connected automatically by price or preference, since they are connected by an architecture of permissions, conventions and privileges that sustains what can circulate and with what efficacy. The passage is long and central: “Politics (in the broad sense of relations, assumptions, and contests pertaining to power) is what links value and exchange in the social life of commodities. In the mundane, day-to-day, small-scale exchanges of things in ordinary life, this fact is not visible, for exchange has the routine and conventionalized look of all customary behavior. But these many ordinary dealings would not be possible were it not for a broad set of agreements concerning what is desirable, what a reasonable ‘exchange of sacrifices’ comprises, and who is permitted to exercise what kind of effective demand in what circumstances. What is political about this process is not just the fact that it signifies and constitutes relations of privilege and social control. What is political about it is the constant tension between the existing frameworks (of price, bargaining, and so forth) and the tendency of commodities to breach these frameworks” <1>Appadurai</1><2>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 57)</2>. In this register, “politics of value” is not a normative addendum, but a description of the engine that makes economic life possible and unstable at the same time. The ordinary economy appears as a field of continuous tension between frames that attempt to stabilize exchange, such as price, bargaining and rules, and the tendency of the flows and disputes themselves to break such frames. Value thus becomes an effect dependent on socially situated agreements and on structures that authorize, block and modulate demand. <3>↩</3>

When, in the work, the authors reach the theme of exclusion, the tone hardens, because the argument depends on treating consumption as access to information and as a practical condition of insertion in networks of support, predictability and opportunity. Exclusion does not appear as a simple lack of goods, but as being out of reach of an informational flow in which one hears and is heard. This loss reconfigures the subject's possible future. The passage formulates this incisively, by directly connecting information, earning potential and “future choosing”. In the original: “To be in control of this sort of information may be vital for getting and keeping a high earning potential. To be outside its range altogether, for the individual who can neither hear it nor make his voice heard, is to risk being treated like a stone, trodden underfoot and kicked aside—a limit to future choosing and the exercise of rational choice. […] One way to keep off the slide from temporary unemployment to unemployability, which leads to chronic isolation, deviance for his children, even criminality, is to be more closely involved with people. And this takes money” <1>Isherwood</1><2>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 63-65)</2>. What is at stake is a theory of the social cost of “being outside”, insofar as non-participation in certain circuits reduces agency by restricting access to signals, alliances and support. The image of the individual “treated like a stone” synthesizes the effect of social illegibility, while the passage ties this effect to a cumulative dynamic, in which exclusion tends to turn into chronic isolation and progressive degradation of opportunities. In this framing, consumption ceases to be read as whim and comes to be read as infrastructure of social survival, since the capacity to maintain bonds and circulate information depends on participating in shared practices that require money. <3>↩</3>

Kopytoff proposes a direct methodological turn. Instead of treating objects as stable units, endowed with a fixed economic “nature”, he suggests tracing trajectories. It is not a matter of writing biography out of literary exoticism, but of showing that the social identity of a thing is constructed and continually reassigned. What makes the biography “cultural” is not the theme, but the perspective, since the object is seen as a culturally constructed entity, invested with specific meanings and subject to successive reclassifications into socially produced categories. The passage formulates this unequivocally: “What would make a biography cultural is not what it deals with, but how and from what perspective. A culturally informed economic biography of an object would look at it as a culturally constructed entity, endowed with culturally specific meanings, and classified and reclassified into culturally constituted categories” <1>Kopytoff</1><2>(Kopytoff, 1986, p. 68)</2>. The reach of the argument lies in shifting the question. Instead of “what is this object?”, the analysis comes to ask through which categories it has passed, who inserted it into them and what kinds of value and prohibition were coupled to each phase. The object ceases to be a neutral support of value and becomes a node of historical classifications, in which “commodity” is only one possibility among others, often a temporary phase. <3>↩</3>

In the chapter <1>The Cultural Biography of Things: Commoditization as Proce</1>ss, part of the volume <2>The Social </2> <3>Life of Things: Commodities in Cultural Perspective</3>, edited by Arjun Appadurai <4>(1986)</4>, Igor Kopytoff <5>(1986)</5> shifts commoditization from a state to a process. Things enter and leave the status of commodity, alternating moments of homogenization and of singularization. <6>↩</6>

One of the most productive points on which Kopytoff's text insists is that the initial exchange does not fix the destiny of the object. Buying, selling or exchanging does not exhaust the subsequent social status of the thing, nor does it guarantee that it remains a commodity in the full sense. Kopytoff describes commoditization as a reversible process full of zones of latency. Things can be withdrawn from the sphere of exchange, “deactivated” as commodities and, even so, retain exchange potential and latent exchange value. The passage is explicit: “In the same way, the fact that an object is bought or exchanged says nothing about its subsequent status and whether it will remain a commodity or not. But unless formally decommoditized, commoditized things remain potential commodities — they continue to have an exchange value, even if they have been effectively withdrawn from their exchange sphere and deactivated, so to speak, as commodities. This deactivation leaves them open not only to the various kinds of singularization I have mentioned so far, but also to individual, as opposed to collective, redefinitions” <1>Kopytoff</1><2>(Kopytoff, 1986, p. 75-76)</2>. The conceptual force lies in breaking the automatic link between “having been a commodity” and “being a commodity”. The thing may remain nominally “possessed” and, at the same time, lose its practical place in the circuit of comparison, equivalence and recognition. The focus ceases to be the moment of purchase and shifts to the maintenance, suspension or reconfiguration of the exchange status and of the kind of value the thing carries at each stage of its trajectory. <3>↩</3>

In discussing singularization, Kopytoff links value and power explicitly. In every society, there are things that are publicly precluded from becoming commodities. Part of these prohibitions is cultural and collectively upheld. In state societies, many are the “handwork of the state”, in a typical combination of what “serves society”, what serves the state and what serves the groups in control. In this scenario, singularization appears as a gesture of authority, since power asserts itself symbolically by insisting on the right to singularize objects, that is, to withdraw them from the common and protect them from the undifferentiated flow of exchange. In the passage: “In every society, there are things that are publicly precluded from being commoditized. Some of the prohibitions are cultural and upheld collectively. In state societies, many of these prohibitions are the handwork of the state, with the usual intertwining between what serves the society at large, what serves the state, and what serves the specific groups in control. […] Power often asserts itself symbolically precisely by insisting on its right to singularize an object, or a set or class of objects” <1>Kopytoff</1><2>(Kopytoff, 1986, p. 73)</2>. The concept of singularization, therefore, is not limited to “making special”. It designates governing the borders between the comparable and the incomparable, between the exchangeable and the safeguarded, between the common and the exceptional. Singularity is a social status with distributive effects, since whoever can singularize can also exclude, hierarchize and stabilize prestige. <3>↩</3>

Kopytoff closes the arc by showing that singularity is not an intimate whim. When singularization is carried out by groups, it carries collective approval, channels the individual drive and gains the weight of “cultural sacredness”. For this reason, disputes over taste, aesthetics and value may conceal conflicts of class, identity and power. At this point, Kopytoff names the institutional core of the process, which is the struggle for control of the “public institutions of singularization”, that is, public arenas capable of certifying and imposing which objects will be treated as singular and which will remain in the common. The passage formulates it precisely: “Singularization of objects by groups within the society poses a special problem. Because it is done by groups, it bears the stamp of collective approval, channels the individual drive for singularization, and takes on the weight of cultural sacredness. […] Behind the extraordinarily vehement assertions of aesthetic values may stand conflicts of culture, class, and ethnic identity, and the struggle over the power of what one might label the ‘public institutions of singularization’” <1>Kopytoff</1><2>(Kopytoff, 1986, p. 81)</2>. The notion of “public institutions of singularization” makes it possible to read value as something that requires certification. Singularity is not “born” of the object. It is produced, validated and disputed in arenas capable of imposing public recognition. For this reason, the cultural biography of a thing changes when these arenas change, since what changes is who holds the power to say what is rare, exceptional, collectible, worthy of reverence or, on the contrary, ordinary and replaceable. <3>↩</3>

“Ritual”, here, is not equivalent to solemnity. It is a social technology for stabilizing meanings. The initial diagnosis is that social life faces a basic problem, since meanings drift, categories dissolve and interpretations slide. Without public conventions, there is no minimum consensual basis for acting. The authors describe rituals as devices that contain this drift and establish visible public definitions. Goods enter as material adjuncts of this process, since they function as a practical support capable of anchoring conventions. The chain appears clearly: “The main problem of social life is to pin down meanings so that they stay still for a little time. Without some conventional ways of selecting and fixing agreed meanings, the minimum consensual basis of society is missing. […] As for tribal society, so too for us: rituals serve to contain the drift of meanings. Rituals are conventions that set up visible public definitions. […] Goods, in this perspective, are ritual adjuncts; consumption is a ritual process whose primary function is to make sense of the inchoate flux of events” <1>Isherwood</1><2>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 43)</2>. Next, consumption is defined in lapidary form as a ritual activity, precisely because it turns fluid judgments into stable and publicized markings: “Consumption uses goods to make firm and visible a particular set of judgments in the fluid processes of classifying persons and events. We have now defined it as a ritual activity” <3>Isherwood</3><4>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 45)</4>. The interpretive key, therefore, is that consuming is not limited to acquiring, but implies participating in a system of marking that fixes classifications. Ritual “makes world” by stabilizing scales of value and recognizable positions. For this reason, repetition is neither noise nor mere habit, since it is part of the mechanism that keeps categories standing over time. <5>↩</5>

It is exactly this point that Grant McCracken systematizes in <1>Culture and Consumption: A Theoretical Account </1> <2>of the Structure and Movement of the Cultural Meaning of Consumer Goods</2> (1986). McCracken begins by pointing to the limitation he considers structural in the dominant approaches of that period. These approaches treated the cultural meaning of goods as something fixed, “adhered” to the object, as if it were stored in it and the consumer only had to buy it to appropriate it. The proposal is to put meaning back in motion. Cultural meaning, in a consumer society, is not a motionless stock, but continuous transit between relatively stable instances and “stations”. For this reason, McCracken speaks of a usual trajectory and of instruments responsible for this displacement. “Cultural meaning in a consumer society moves ceaselessly from one location to another. In the usual trajectory, cultural meaning moves first from the culturally constituted world to consumer goods and then from these goods to the individual consumer. Several instruments are responsible for this movement: advertising, the fashion system, and four consumption rituals” <3>McCracken</3><4>(McCracken, 1986, p. 71)</4>. Thus, in the first place, “good” and “consumer” cease to be origins of meaning and become points of passage, with specific functions in symbolic circulation. In the second place, the circuit is not merely metaphorical, since there are identifiable instruments that transfer meaning, such as advertising, the fashion system and rituals. With this, culture does not appear as a diffuse backdrop, but as a mechanism that must be operated for meaning to move and remain functional. <5>↩</5>

In dealing with the instruments that transfer meaning from the “culturally constituted world” to goods, McCracken assigns to advertising a stronger role than that of “persuading”. Advertising is described as a conduit, that is, a channel through which meaning continually “pours”. It couples meanings to goods, removes old meanings and attaches new ones. The viewer or reader enters as an active participant in the process, because he must decode and complete the transfer. It follows that advertising continually informs the public of the “present state” of the cultural meaning available in goods, as if it updated the symbolic inventory of the material world. The passage is entirely designed for this effect: “Advertising is a conduit through which meaning constantly pours from the culturally constituted world to consumer goods. Through advertising, old and new goods continually give up old meanings and take on new ones. As active participants in this process, the viewer/reader is kept informed of the present state and stock of cultural meaning that exists in consumer goods. To this extent, advertising serves as a lexicon of current cultural meanings” <1>McCracken</1><2>(McCracken, 1986, p. 75-76)</2>. The vocabulary employed is revealing, since it points to updating, and not to a mere message. Advertising, in this key, functions as a mechanism of symbolic synchronization. It keeps the public aligned with the prevailing repertoire and reorganizes the legibility of what goods “mean” at a given moment. <3>↩</3>

Before examining the instruments, McCracken defines the place where meaning originally resides. He locates it in the “culturally constituted world” and does so through a double definition of culture, crucial for refusing the idea of culture as a mere subjective filter. Culture appears as lens and as blueprint. It functions as lens because it guides how the phenomenon is seen. It functions as blueprint because it prescribes coordinates of action and production, by specifying behaviors and objects that become legitimate references. The passage makes this double function explicit: “Culture constitutes the phenomenal world in two ways. First, culture is the ‘lens’ through which the individual views phenomena […]. Second, culture is the ‘blueprint’ of human activity, determining the co-ordinates of social action and productive activity, and specifying the behaviors and objects that issue from both. […] In short, culture constitutes the world by supplying it with meaning. This meaning can be characterized in terms of two concepts: cultural categories and cultural principles” <1>McCracken</1><2>(McCracken, 1986, p. 72)</2>. cultural configure the map of the intelligible, by ordering divisions of time, space, person, status, gender, class and appropriateness. It is not a matter of individual opinion, but of a matrix that guides perception and, at the same time, defines a repertoire of actions and objects that can count as socially relevant. <3>↩</3>

The theory of the transit of meaning contains a decisive point. Part of meaning is perishable. McCracken uses this notion to explain why symbolic appropriation is not exhausted at purchase and why consumption rituals must be repeated. If meaning “expires”, it must be periodically extracted from possessions, since symbolic life requires reactivation. For this reason, he links perishability to the need for a continuous process of transfer from the good to the consumer and, consequently, to the tendency to resort to specific rituals, such as grooming rituals. These rituals involve care and “work” to make symbolic properties “live”, even if only for a short time. The passage is long and very clear: “It is clear that some of the cultural meaning drawn from goods has a perishable nature. As a result, the consumer must draw cultural meaning out of his/her possessions on a repeated basis. When a continual process of meaning transfer from goods to consumer is necessary, the consumer will likely resort to a grooming ritual. The purpose of this ritual is to take the special pains necessary to insure that the special, perishable properties […] are, as it were, ‘coaxed’ out of their resident goods and made to live, however briefly and precariously, in the life of the individual consumer” <1>McCracken</1><2>(McCracken, 1986, p. 79)</2>. The image of “coaxed” is central, since it indicates that meaning does not emerge on its own. It must be activated and cultivated. The very precariousness expressed in “however briefly and precariously” reinforces the logic of continuous maintenance. Ritualized consumption thus appears as regular symbolic work, and not as whim. Repetition, in this framing, is the ordinary way of preventing fragile cultural attributes from collapsing through obsolescence, disuse or replacement by new arrangements of meaning. <3>↩</3>

The dismantling of “demand” as a private impulse appears when Appadurai contrasts mechanisms that manufacture taste and regulate appropriateness of consumption in different societies. The target is the idea that desiring and demanding would be spontaneous movements of the individual, like a psychological energy that the economy would merely account for. Appadurai describes demand as a socially regulated and socially generated impulse, produced by taste-making mechanisms and by rules that organize the appropriate, the available and the prestigious. Even when the mechanisms vary, whether by fashion, media, informal norms or sumptuary laws, the structure remains. Demand is born within devices of social regulation and production, and not as an artifact of individual whims or needs. In the passage: “The demand for commodities is critically regulated by this variety of taste-making mechanisms, whose social origin is more clearly understood (both by consumers and by analysts) in our own society than in those distant from us. […] In both cases, however, demand is a socially regulated and generated impulse, not an artifact of individual whims or needs” <1>Appadurai</1><2>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 32)</2>. In this way, demand ceases to be a natural given and becomes an institutional and cultural variable. What counts as desirable, comparable and legitimate is not merely perceived, but produced and stabilized by mechanisms that organize visibility, appropriateness, distinction and belonging. The economy of consumption becomes legible as a process of manufacturing criteria, and not as a sum of autonomous wills. <3>↩</3>

With the reconstruction of the techno-media ambience concluded, the focus shifts to the political economy of digital platforms. The point now is to make explicit the mode of production in which these mediations operate. Drawing on Varoufakis <1>(2024)</1>, Dowbor <2>(2025)</2> and Marx <3>(2011; 2013)</3>, an arrangement is described in which platforms combine infrastructural dependence, informational rentierism, deliberate production of artificial scarcity and continuous extraction of value. These dynamics do not hover above the service: they materialize in business architecture, private governance and the functional design of digital goods and services.

Business activity organizes factors of production and subjects them to a rationality of viability, expansion and preservation of the business. In contemporary capitalism, this rationality operates under permanent tension: on the one hand, it demands responsiveness to market expectations; on the other, it intensifies profit maximization through revenue expansion, selective cost management, containment of uncertainties and active minimization of risks.

This dynamic projects, within the firm, a permanent imperative to govern contingencies, foreseeing, calibrating and redistributing whatever may affect the stability of the business. The decisive point is that this risk governance rarely remains confined to the organization. It tends to operate through mechanisms of displacement, transferring relevant portions of risk and social cost to third parties and to the State, which is often called upon only afterwards to restore the broken balance.

<1>p. 140</1> The distinction between internal and external risks makes this rationality explicit. Internal risks are those that bear directly on the performance of the enterprise: production chain, logistics, quality standards, reputation and organizational capacity. As a rule, they remain manageable by the firm, since they depend on governance, compliance, investment in quality and operational control. External risks, although they may be triggered by economic activity, manifest themselves more diffusely and outside the supplier's immediate sphere of control. They reach the health, integrity, assets, privacy, lifetime and informational environment of consumers, as well as competitors, communities and institutional ecosystems. They also include costs of redress, oversight and containment shifted to the public sphere.

It is in the domain of external risks that the paradoxical dimension of the “perfect business” becomes evident: an operation capable of maximizing gains while keeping under control, at least from the business point of view, the risks that threaten its own stability. This threshold can never be reduced to zero, as the consumerist theory of quality recognizes by admitting the inevitability of failures and the need for preventive and remedial discipline of supply. The problem begins when the internal minimization of risk is obtained through the diffuse transfer of its effects to consumers, society and the State.

The managerial reading that reduces the firm to the abstract pursuit of profit obscures the concrete way in which that profit is produced. The firm does not maximize results merely by producing more or selling better; it maximizes results by designing structures that organize responsibilities, filter obligations and distribute burdens. Profit therefore depends on strategies of risk allocation. For this reason, Consumer Law, when it intervenes in the market, is not confined to punishing harm already done.

By establishing minimum standards of adequacy and safety, Consumer Law functions as a legal check on the tendency toward externalization. The supplier is liable because it occupies the structural position of the party that reaps the gains of the activity and must therefore internalize the cost of the risks it creates, preventively and, when necessary, through effective redress.

The industrialist who operates in the food market must ensure, as a condition of the viability of the business, that the product lives up at least minimally to what it promises. Adequacy is not reduced to immediate performance, such as taste, preservation or appearance; it includes safety and quality over time, so that the product does not harm the consumer's physical, psychological or financial integrity. At this point, the State not only may intervene: it must set minimum parameters and hold the supplier liable when they are breached. Regulation and liability function as an institutional response to external <1>p. 141</1> risk. What, from the business point of view, could be treated as an avoidable cost appears, from the legal point of view, as socially inadmissible harm and as a burden that must be internalized by whoever structures and benefits from the economic activity.

The problem is reconfigured when emerging techniques redesign the market and introduce, on a mass scale, new goods, services and forms of risk. With each innovation that reorganizes the consumption experience, a pattern of supply is instituted that is not immediately intelligible through traditional categories: the way of offering changes, the way of enjoying changes, the mechanisms of value capture change and, above all, the ways in which risk is distributed change.

A specific challenge then arises for Consumer Law. It is not enough to recognize the new object in circulation; it is necessary to understand the techno-media grammar that makes it consumable, desirable and, at the same time, opaque. In the classical industrial paradigm, social and legal inspection of risk can bear on the materiality of the product, such as composition, performance and safety. In the techno-media order, risk tends to shift to conditions of access, regimes of governance, decision architectures and to the semiotic layer that sustains the promise of consumption.

For this reason, the political economy reconstructed here must advance to the point at which perceived value, belonging and recognition are understood as dimensions administered within the ecosystem. It is in this grammar that continuous extraction becomes practicable: the platform captures value because it governs not only transactions, but the conditions of intelligibility, desire and permanence that make the transaction recurrent.

Contemporary business rationality finds there a particularly acute zone of friction. Internal risks remain relatively controllable by management and quality; external risks, in techno-mediated markets, depend on collective recognition and institutional interpretation. The difficulty lies in identifying when a practice transfers an excessive burden to the consumer or produces harm without presenting itself as classic physical or patrimonial injury. In environments organized by technical layers and interface languages, externalization tends to operate through indirect and diffuse routes, in the form of informational asymmetry, opacity of criteria, absence of auditability and loss of control over one's own consumption experience. Hence the need for categories capable of seeing, beyond the product in the narrow sense, the regimes of promise, access and governance that configure contemporary consumption.

The discussion of risk and externalization, therefore, does not function as a generic prologue, but as an entry into the political economy of platforms. When value is produced in <1>p. 142</1> mediating ecosystems, the rationality of minimizing uncertainties and shifting costs tends to be incorporated into the very architecture of the business. The platform becomes simultaneously the place of the offer and the place of administration of the conditions of enjoyment. With this, the possibility of shifting burdens onto the consumer and onto the public sphere intensifies.

From a macroeconomic perspective, Yanis Varoufakis <1>(2024)</1> stands out for analysing what he considers a paradigm shift in the global economic landscape. He argues that the capitalist system is on its way to being replaced by what he calls “technofeudalism”, in which capital no longer presents itself primarily as material property and comes to be concentrated “in the cloud”, that is, in digital assets, online platforms and algorithms. The critique deserves recognition for stressing that this cloud capital, held by those he categorizes as “cloudalists” (our translation of “<2>nubelistas</2>”, from the Spanish edition), is characterized by its capacity to reproduce itself without generating proportional extra costs for its owners. Extraction thus expands over those the author describes as “cloud serfs”, subjects who figure simultaneously as consumers and as continuous suppliers of two raw materials essential to the system: data and attention.

From a Brazilian standpoint, Ladislau Dowbor <1>(2025)</1> stands out for his critique of what he calls “rentier capitalism”, a transformative system that, in his account, has redesigned global dynamics and marked a significant break with earlier modes of production. According to the author, this evolution can be described in three broad historical phases. In agrarian societies, domination fell to landowners, who controlled the available resources through force and religious authority. The industrial revolution introduced machines and factories, shifting power to industrial capitalists. In this period, the exploitation of labor tied directly to the production of goods becomes visible, creating a tangible connection between labor, output and public services. The modern digital era, in turn, rests on an economy based on knowledge and information, in which platforms such as <2>Google</2> and <3>Amazon</3> dominate through informational instrumentalization, which has become the most valuable resource.

Dowbor identifies rentier capitalism as a system in which power resides in the possession and control of assets, rather than in the production of goods. Read in this key, platforms such as <1>Facebook</1>, according to the author, exemplify the phenomenon through “demand monopolies”, forcing users to depend on certain services because of their broad social adoption. The system, in his account, depends on financialization, a process that decouples money from real economic activity and enables the continuous extraction of wealth. The author draws on examples such as developing nations trapped in debt cycles by exorbitant interest and individuals <2>p. 143</2> burdened by expensive credit. Absentee owners, such as <3>hedge</3> funds and investment firms, are said to concentrate the financial returns and neglect the social impacts. In this context, Dowbor criticizes the legislative framework of intellectual property, arguing that it has become a barrier to innovation and ceased to operate as an instrument of progress.

Against this background, it becomes possible to shift the focus from the “medium” to the “mode of production” crystallized in platforms. It is not enough to describe technologies and symbolic mediations. What matters is to understand which form of economic organization is condensed in the architecture of these infrastructures and what place it reserves for the consumer and for digital goods. The aim here is to offer vocabulary for treating digitally based businesses not as simple contractual models (“subscription”, “<1>freemium</1>”, “advertising”, “microtransactions” etc.), but as manifestations of a common structural arrangement, marked by platform technofeudalism, digital rentierism and a specific form of exploitation of the consumer who, contextually, is also characterized as an incorporated external labor force (the “consumer-worker”).

Looking at these business categories from this angle, one does not obtain a neutral classification of forms of monetization. One obtains a map of how the functional architecture of digital goods is designed to enable the continuous extraction of value. Each apparently technical option<1><2>116</2></1> is part of an underlying economic project. The unity of this project becomes more visible when three levels are brought back together. At the macro level, Varoufakis describes platforms operating as cloud technofiefs. At the meso level, Dowbor emphasizes digital rentierism and the toll economy. At the micro level, Marx provides the key to perceiving how digital consumption can function as the invisible labor of a contemporary kind of “informational lumpenproletariat”.

The triad is decisive because it allows us to understand why the Immaterial Object of Consumption must be treated as an infrastructure concept, and not merely as a label for digital goods. It makes explicit that the ontological failure of the CDC is not merely conceptual carelessness, but blindness before a mode of production that reorganizes the very form of exploitation.

Articulated, the three dimensions<1><2>117</2></1> make it possible to reclassify digitally based businesses as architectures of continuous extraction of value, operating on functionally <3>p. 144</3> defined immaterial goods. This is a reclassification that provides theoretical grounding for questioning the potential unlawfulness of the intentions and purposes embedded in the <4>design</4> of platforms. If the platform mode of production depends structurally on producing artificial scarcity over informational goods and on establishing economic and symbolic captivity over the consumer-worker, it is revealed in the operative purpose with which the business architecture is designed.

The large platforms that operate attention ecosystems (here called cloudalists and subcloudalists) are not limited to offering products or services. They build, around their users, environments of continuous audiovisual distraction. Their business models start from meticulously studied consumption profiles and position the individual within a gravitational field of signs. Games, series, songs, competitive broadcasts, advertising campaigns and licensed products make up a constellation that accompanies the subject throughout everyday life. The result is a global positioning of the brand and its digital goods, such that it becomes difficult to experience digital life outside the contours of this ecosystem.

Symbols endowed with value in the collective imagination can be captured, recombined and protected under intellectual property regimes that favor the economic exploiter, even though the composition of this symbolic capital depends on diffuse contributions. The asymmetry becomes more evident when one observes that the legal order itself recognizes, in certain segments, remedies of subsequent economic participation. The resale right, granted to sculptors and visual artists, exemplifies a mechanism by which creators retain a limited share in the subsequent economic fruits of their work. The reference is not meant to transplant the institution automatically, but to indicate that the full concentration of gains derived from collectively fed symbolic chains is not a legal inevitability. In attention ecosystems, the social function of intellectual property requires at least that the question be raised again about the limits of the full appropriation of value by a single entity when the economic chain depends structurally on authors, artists, communities and consumers.

The maintenance of models in which a single entity concentrates, by business decision and legal <1>design</1>, the totality of gains derived from the economic exploitation of narrative universes built by collective efforts strains the principles of objective good faith and contractual balance. The social function of intellectual property, in a scenario of cloudalists and attention monopoly, requires reconsidering to what extent it is admissible for the exclusive holder to accumulate in full the profits of value chains that depend, structurally, on the diffuse contribution of authors, artists, communities and consumers.

<1>p. 145</1> The decisive point is that the illustrative scenario does not describe a sectoral anomaly of entertainment, but a general form of economic organization through infrastructure. The capacity to maintain “nominal ownership” and, at the same time, downgrade the enjoyment bundle through unilateral updating, as well as the power to impose sanctions that degrade reputation, visibility and access, reveals that the platform not only offers a good, but administers a territory of circulation of signs, time and payment. At this point, the distinction between nominal title and the effective enjoyment bundle is decisive. On platforms, the formal permanence of the item in the account does not guarantee the preservation of its functional, symbolic or economic value. The object may continue to “exist” for accounting and contractual purposes, while the architecture that gave it utility, distinction or recognition is reconfigured by the supplier.

If in the first part of the discussion the focus fell on technique, media and design as forms of everyday governance, the next step is to make explicit the economic rationality that makes this governance profitable and structural. The anthropology of consumption will enter, along this path, as analytical support for understanding how the visible and the desirable also become economically governed dimensions. Before that, however, it is necessary to show how the architecture of the ecosystem converts dependence and permanence into continuous extraction of value.

Contemporary digital consumption can no longer be adequately understood as the simple acquisition of a thing or the contracting of a one-off service. In many ecosystems, the experience takes the form of permanence in a governed environment, in which the interface organizes access, induces choices, limits alternatives and distributes rewards or sanctions. The decisive shift occurs when mediation ceases to be perceived as a neutral channel and comes to operate as a form of organization of experience. In this regime, technique and media constitute practical ambiences: they frame the possible, define the relevant and stabilize certain conducts as normal through repetition, convenience and design.

This ambience is also inseparable from an economic architecture of its own. Digital platforms are not limited to connecting users and offers. They organize markets, administer access, structure dependencies and convert circulation into continuous extraction of value. Infrastructure, data, interface and operating rules come to compose a single arrangement, in which performance is prolonged, the bond is renewed by frictions and incentives, and the capture of attention and diffuse productivity is part of the ordinary functioning of the service. Economic rationality materializes in design, in curation and in execution protocols, so that competition comes to be fought also over the control of ecosystems, exit costs and the administration of visibility.

To describe this background without turning it into mere sociological impression, three conceptual sets are mobilized, each with its own function. The first reconstructs the passage of technique and media from tools to environments of life, in which efficiency, automatism and integration act as criteria of social organization, without eliminating the institutional dispute over design and governance. On this axis, Jacques Ellul<1><2>28</2></1>, Neil Postman<3><4>29</4></3> <5>p. 84</5> and Willem H. Vanderburg<6><7>30</7></6> provide the diagnosis of the techno-media ambience, while Andrew Feenberg<8><9>31</9></8> introduces the critical key needed to set aside determinism and preserve the controllability of technical choices.

The second set reconstructs the political economy of platforms as an arrangement of extraction, toll and dependence, in which digital infrastructures function as private territories of market administration, coordination of supply and capture of distributed value. Yanis Varoufakis<1><2>32</2></1> and Ladislau Dowbor<3><4>33</4></3> offer the main lenses of this reconstruction, in dialogue with the critique of political economy and with categories of Karl Marx<5><6>34</6></5> mobilized to clarify the technical and economic form of extraction in digital environments.

The third set operates as a bridge between political economy and the semiotics of consumption, describing how value, belonging and recognition become organizing components of experience and practical conditions for stabilizing extraction. At this point, the anthropology of consumption, drawn from Mary Douglas<1><2>35</2></1>, Baron Isherwood<3><4>36</4></3>, Arjun <5>p. 85</5> Appadurai<6><7>37</7></6>, Igor Kopytoff<8><9>38</9></8> and Grant McCraken<10><11>39</11></10>, makes it possible to understand that consumed objects circulate not only on account of utility or price, but through regimes of meaning that sustain attachment, distinction and permanence.

This path yields a structural framework capable of making the legal problem visible without depending on impressionistic descriptions of particular cases. When technique operates as environment and the platform operates as market architecture, the consumer relationship comes to be traversed by regimes of access, data, interface and technical and legal exclusivities that condition delivery, enjoyment and the effective space of choice. It is this background that supports the formulation of categories capable of rendering attributable and controllable the losses and asymmetries that, under a strictly material ontology of consumption, would tend to appear as “system change”, “normal update” or “inevitable service event”.
